title: Enhanced Analysis of Electrophysiological Data from High-Density Multi-Electrode Arrays
author: Wolff, Polito, et al.

steps.title: Culture mESC lines on laminin
steps.instruction: Culture E14 mouse embryonic stem cells (mESC) on laminin‑coated dishes and WT‑B1 mESCs on mitomycin‑treated MEF feeder layers in ES medium.

steps.title: Plate mESCs at low density
steps.instruction: The day before differentiation, plate the mESC lines at low density on laminin‑coated dishes.

steps.title: Switch to DDM medium with B27
steps.instruction: The day after plating, culture the cells in DDM medium supplemented with B27‑without‑vitamin‑A as previously reported.

steps.title: Add DMH1‑HCl (1 µM) days 0‑8
steps.instruction: From day 0 to day 8 of culture, supplement the DDM medium with the dorsomorphin analog DMH1‑HCl at a final concentration of 1 µM (replace cyclopamine).

steps.title: Plate neuroprogenitors on PEI/laminin chips
steps.instruction: At 12 days of 2D in‑vitro corticogenesis, plate E14 or WT‑B1 neuroprogenitor cells on Accura chips (3Brain) coated with 0.1 mg ml⁻¹ poly‑ethylene‑imine (PEI) and 33 µg ml⁻¹ laminin, following the manufacturer’s instructions.

steps.title: Differentiate to DIV 21 then extend culture
steps.instruction: Differentiate the cells until day‑in‑vitro 21 (DIV 21), then maintain them in complete Neurobasal medium for an additional 21 days. The entire in‑vitro corticogenesis protocol spans approximately 7 weeks.

steps.title: Maintain culture conditions and medium
steps.instruction: During differentiation keep cultures at 37 °C in a 5 % CO₂ atmosphere; filter the complete Neurobasal medium with a 0.22 µm bottle‑top filter, store the filtered medium at 4 °C, and use it within 1 week.

steps.title: Test for mycoplasma regularly
steps.instruction: Control the samples regularly to exclude mycoplasma contamination, e.g., by using the MycoSPY kit.

steps.title: Freeze cells for storage
steps.instruction: To store cells, supplement ES medium with 10 % DMSO, freeze the suspension at –80 °C overnight, then transfer to –196 °C for long‑term storage.

steps.title: Analyze HD‑MEA data with spikeNburst/nicespike
steps.instruction: Using the exported data from the 3Brain HD‑MEA system (4,096 electrodes), run spike sorting, burst detection, and synchrony analyses with the spikeNburst and nicespike graphical user interfaces, applying the parameters described in the protocol’s tables.

description: This protocol outlines the steps for analyzing raw voltage recordings of extracellular electrophysiological activity from high-density multi-electrode array (HD-MEA) systems with exceptional spatial and temporal resolution,1,2,3 integrating state-of-the-art spike sorting, burst detection, and synchrony measures within an accessible and flexible framework. It was adapted to analyze in vitro neuronal culture recordings from the 3Brain device, which comprises 4,096 electrodes. However, we highlight the versatility of the protocol for analysis of recordings from different HD-MEAs by minimal adaptations of the open-source software. The spiking activity of individual neurons is detected by a process called spike sorting,4,5,6,7,8 which, applied on HD-MEA data, has resulted in advances in the characterization of neuronal growth, connectivity, and plasticity.2,9,10 The demand of fast, reliable, and reproducible HD-MEA results is still unmet. Analyzing these extensive datasets presents challenges, such as artifact removal, spike sorting, and accurate assessment of neuronal synchronization.11,12 Moreover, the management of spike sorting methods is time-consuming and technically complex, resulting in limited user access and loss of data reproducibility. Existing software solutions, including the default tools integrated within standard analytical platforms, such as Brainwave13 from 3Brain, primarily provide fundamental spike detection functionalities which are restricted to single-channel analyses. This limitation often results in overestimation of neuronal units and network activity due to redundant measurements of neurons being simultaneously recorded by multiple electrodes. Furthermore, while effective for systems with few electrodes, analysis tools such as Spycode14 and MEA-NAP15 are neither scalable nor compatible with contemporary HD-MEA datasets.
